nodes.title: What is the rule for determining outliers in a boxplot?
nodes.F: Calculate IQR = Q3 - Q1. Lower Bound: Q1 - 1.5(IQR). Upper Bound: Q3 + 1.5(IQR). Any data point outside this is an outlier.
nodes.I: Calculate IQR = Q3 - Q1. Lower Bound: Q1 - 1.5(IQR). Upper Bound: Q3 + 1.5(IQR). Any data point outside this is an outlier.

nodes.title: When should you use Median over Mean?
nodes.I: Use Median for skewed distributions or those with outliers, as it is a resistant measure of center.

nodes.title: What are the proportions of the Empirical Rule?
nodes.F: For Normal distributions: 68% within 1sigma, 95% within 2sigma, 99.7% within 3sigma.
nodes.K: For Normal distributions: 68% within 1sigma, 95% within 2sigma, 99.7% within 3sigma.
nodes.I: For Normal distributions: 68% within 1sigma, 95% within 2sigma, 99.7% within 3sigma.

nodes.title: How do you calculate a residual?
nodes.F: Residual = Actual (y) - Predicted (y-hat). Mnemonic: RAP (Residual = Actual - Predicted).
nodes.I: Residual = Actual (y) - Predicted (y-hat). Mnemonic: RAP (Residual = Actual - Predicted).

nodes.title: What is the interpretation of r^2 (Coefficient of Determination)?
nodes.F: "r^2 percent of the variation in the [response variable] is accounted for by the linear model relating it to the [explanatory variable]."
nodes.I: "r^2 percent of the variation in the [response variable] is accounted for by the linear model relating it to the [explanatory variable]."

nodes.title: What is the definition of an influential point in regression?
nodes.I: A point that, if removed, significantly changes the slope, y-intercept, or correlation coefficient.

nodes.title: What is the difference between a histogram and a bar chart?
nodes.I: Histograms are for quantitative data (bins touch); bar charts are for categorical data (bars don't touch).

nodes.title: What does the standard deviation of residuals (s) represent?
nodes.I: The typical size of the "error" (prediction vertical distance) when using the LSRL to predict Y from X.

nodes.title: What happens to the mean and standard deviation if you multiply every value by a constant?
nodes.I: Both the mean and standard deviation are multiplied by that constant.

nodes.title: What is the y-intercept interpretation in context?
nodes.I: The predicted value of Y when X is zero. Often has no practical meaning if X=0 is outside the data range.

nodes.title: What is the "Standard Error of the Slope"?
nodes.I: It estimates how much the slope of the LSRL varies from sample to sample.

nodes.title: What is conditional relative frequency?
nodes.I: The value in a specific cell divided by the total of its row or column.

nodes.title: What is back-to-back stemplot used for?
nodes.I: Comparing the distributions of two quantitative variables side-by-side.

nodes.title: What is the goal of a Simple Random Sample (SRS)?
nodes.F: To give every group of size n an equal chance of being selected, reducing bias.
nodes.I: To give every group of size n an equal chance of being selected, reducing bias.

nodes.title: Define Cluster Sampling.
nodes.I: Splitting the population into heterogeneous groups (clusters) and randomly selecting entire clusters.

nodes.title: Why is random assignment used in experiments?
nodes.I: To create roughly equivalent groups and balance the effects of confounding variables.

nodes.title: What is the purpose of a control group?
nodes.I: To provide a baseline for comparison to see if the treatment has a real effect.

nodes.title: Define Undercoverage bias.
nodes.I: When some members of the population are left out of the process of choosing the sample.

nodes.title: Define Response bias.
nodes.I: When the behavior of the interviewer or the wording of the question influences the answers.

nodes.title: What is "Blocking" in an experiment?
nodes.I: Grouping similar experimental units together to reduce the variability of the response variable.

nodes.title: When can you generalize results to a population?
nodes.I: When the individuals were randomly selected from that population.

nodes.title: What is a sampling frame?
nodes.I: The actual list of individuals from which the sample is drawn.

nodes.title: What is systematic random sampling?
nodes.F: Selecting every kth individual from a list after a random starting point.
nodes.I: Selecting every kth individual from a list after a random starting point.

nodes.title: Does a large sample size reduce bias?
nodes.I: No. If the sampling method is biased (like voluntary response), a large sample just gives a more "precise" biased result.

nodes.title: What is a factor in an experiment?
nodes.I: The explanatory variable (e.g., dosage).

nodes.title: What is the scope of inference?
nodes.I: The limit of who the results apply to and whether cause-and-effect can be claimed.

nodes.title: Define Mutually Exclusive (Disjoint) events.
nodes.F: Events that cannot happen at the same time. P(A AND B) = 0.
nodes.I: Events that cannot happen at the same time. P(A AND B) = 0.

nodes.title: What is the test for Independence?
nodes.F: P(A|B) = P(A) or P(A AND B) = P(A) * P(B).
nodes.I: P(A|B) = P(A) or P(A AND B) = P(A) * P(B).

nodes.title: Define Expected Value (E(X) or mux).
nodes.F: The long-run average of a random variable: Sum [x * P(x)].
nodes.I: The long-run average of a random variable: Sum [x * P(x)].

nodes.title: How do you calculate Binomial probability for exactly k successes?
nodes.K: Use binompdf(n, p, k) on the calculator.
nodes.I: Use binompdf(n, p, k) on the calculator.

nodes.title: What are the BITS conditions for a Geometric distribution?
nodes.I: Binary, Independent, Trials until first success, Same probability.

nodes.title: How do you calculate the standard deviation of a Binomial distribution?
nodes.I: sigma = sqrt(np(1-p)).

nodes.title: If you combine two independent random variables X and Y, how do you find the new variance?
nodes.F: sigma^2X +/- Y = sigma^2X + sigma^2Y. (Variances always add).
nodes.I: sigma^2X +/- Y = sigma^2X + sigma^2Y. (Variances always add).

nodes.title: What must the sum of probabilities in a discrete distribution be?
nodes.I: Exactly 1.

nodes.title: Define a "Random Variable".
nodes.I: A numerical outcome of a random process.

nodes.title: Does P(X = k) matter in a continuous distribution?
nodes.F: No, P(X = k) = 0 for any single point in a continuous distribution.
nodes.I: No, P(X = k) = 0 for any single point in a continuous distribution.

nodes.title: What is the "10% Condition" for independence when sampling?
nodes.F: When sampling without replacement, you can assume trials are independent if n <= 0.10N.
nodes.I: When sampling without replacement, you can assume trials are independent if n <= 0.10N.

nodes.title: How do you find P(A AND B) for independent events?
nodes.I: P(A) * P(B).

nodes.title: What is a Sampling Distribution?
nodes.I: The distribution of all possible values of a statistic from all possible samples of the same size.

nodes.title: What is a P-value?
nodes.I: The probability of getting a result as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

nodes.title: If P-value > alpha, what is the conclusion?
nodes.F: Fail to reject H0; there is not enough evidence for Ha.
nodes.I: Fail to reject H0; there is not enough evidence for Ha.

nodes.title: What is a Type II Error?
nodes.F: Failing to reject H0 when it is actually false (False Negative).
nodes.I: Failing to reject H0 when it is actually false (False Negative).

nodes.title: How do you interpret a Confidence Interval?
nodes.I: "We are 95% confident that the interval from [Low] to [High] captures the true [parameter in context]."

nodes.title: What happens to an interval as sample size increases?
nodes.I: The interval gets narrower.

nodes.title: What are the three conditions for inference?
nodes.F: Random, Independent (10%), and Normal (Large Counts or n >= 30).
nodes.K: Random, Independent (10%), and Normal (Large Counts or n >= 30).
nodes.I: Random, Independent (10%), and Normal (Large Counts or n >= 30).

nodes.title: What is "Power" in a significance test?
nodes.I: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.

nodes.title: What is the null hypothesis for a Chi-Square Test of Independence?
nodes.I: There is no association between the two variables in the population.

nodes.title: How do you calculate degrees of freedom for Chi-Square Independence?
nodes.I: df = (rows - 1)(cols - 1).

nodes.title: What is the point estimate?
nodes.F: The sample statistic (x-bar or p-hat) used to estimate the population parameter.
nodes.I: The sample statistic (x-bar or p-hat) used to estimate the population parameter.

nodes.title: What is the null hypothesis for a test of slope?
nodes.I: H0: beta = 0 (No linear relationship).

nodes.title: How do you calculate "Expected Counts" for Chi-Square?
nodes.I: (Row Total * Column Total) / Grand Total.

nodes.title: What is a statistic?
nodes.I: A number that describes a sample (e.g., x-bar or p-hat).

nodes.title: Define an unbiased estimator.
nodes.I: A statistic whose sampling distribution's mean is equal to the true parameter being estimated.

nodes.title: What is the formula for the standard deviation of p-hat?
nodes.I: sqrt( p(1-p) / n ).

nodes.title: What is the formula for the standard deviation of x-bar?
nodes.I: sigma / sqrt(n).

nodes.title: What does the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) say about the shape of x-bar?
nodes.K: If n >= 30, the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately Normal regardless of the population shape.
nodes.I: If n >= 30, the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately Normal regardless of the population shape.

nodes.title: What are the mean and standard deviation of the difference in sample means (x-bar1 - x-bar2)?
nodes.I: Mean = mu1 - mu2; SD = sqrt( (sigma1^2 / n1) + (sigma2^2 / n2) ).

nodes.title: How do you check if the distribution of p-hat is approximately Normal?
nodes.C: Check the Large Counts condition: np >= 10 and n(1-p) >= 10.
nodes.I: Check the Large Counts condition: np >= 10 and n(1-p) >= 10.

nodes.title: What is a "Critical Value" (z* or t*)?
nodes.I: The number of standard errors you must move from the mean to capture a specific area of confidence.

nodes.title: What is the formula for a one-sample z-interval for a proportion?
nodes.I: p-hat +/- z* * sqrt( p-hat(1 - p-hat) / n ).

nodes.title: How do you find the sample size n needed for a specific margin of error (ME) for a proportion?
nodes.I: n = (z* / ME)^2 * p*(1-p*). Use p*=0.5 if no estimate is given.

nodes.title: What is the Test Statistic formula for a one-proportion z-test?
nodes.I: z = (p-hat - p-zero) / sqrt( p-zero(1 - p-zero) / n ). Note: Use p-zero in the denominator.

nodes.title: What is "Pooling" in a two-proportion z-test?
nodes.I: Combining successes and sample sizes from both groups to get a single p-hat-combined when H0 assumes p1 = p2.

nodes.title: What is the Large Counts condition for a two-proportion z-interval?
nodes.I: n1p-hat1, n1(1-p-hat1), n2p-hat2, and n2(1-p-hat2) must all be >= 10.

nodes.title: Why use the T-distribution instead of Normal for means?
nodes.I: Because we use s-x to estimate sigma, which adds extra variability.

nodes.title: What is the formula for a one-sample t-interval for a mean?
nodes.I: x-bar +/- t* * (s-x / sqrt(n)).

nodes.title: What is the "Normal/Large Sample" condition for means?
nodes.K: Population is Normal, OR n >= 30, OR a graph of sample data shows no strong skew/outliers.
nodes.I: Population is Normal, OR n >= 30, OR a graph of sample data shows no strong skew/outliers.

nodes.title: What is a "Matched Pairs" t-procedure?
nodes.I: When data comes from two measurements on the same person or twins; you analyze the single list of differences.

nodes.title: What is the Null Hypothesis for a two-sample t-test?
nodes.I: H0: mu1 = mu2 (or mu1 - mu2 = 0).

nodes.title: If the 95% confidence interval for mu1-mu2 is (2, 10), is there evidence of a difference?
nodes.I: Yes, because zero is not in the interval.

nodes.title: Do we usually pool for t-tests?
nodes.I: No, the AP exam and modern statistics recommend "Pooled: No" for means.

nodes.title: How do you interpret the standard deviation of the differences (s-diff) in matched pairs?
nodes.I: The typical distance of an individual difference from the mean difference.

nodes.title: What are the three types of Chi-Square tests?
nodes.I: Goodness of Fit, Homogeneity, and Independence.

nodes.title: What does a Test for Homogeneity test?
nodes.I: If the distribution of one categorical variable is the same across multiple populations/groups.

nodes.title: What is the Chi-Square test statistic formula?
nodes.I: Chi-sq = Sum of [ (Observed - Expected)^2 / Expected ].

nodes.title: What is the shape of a Chi-Square distribution?
nodes.I: Right-skewed and always positive.

nodes.title: What are the conditions for Chi-Square?
nodes.I: Random, Independent (10%), and Large Counts (all Expected counts >= 5).

nodes.title: What is a "Cell Contribution" in Chi-Square?
nodes.I: The value (Obs-Exp)^2 / Exp for a single cell; it shows which category deviated most.

nodes.title: How does the TI-84 calculate Expected counts for Independence?
nodes.K: It does it automatically and stores them in Matrix after you run the test.
nodes.I: It does it automatically and stores them in Matrix after you run the test.

nodes.title: What is the Alternative Hypothesis for all Chi-Square tests?
nodes.I: Ha: The null is not correct (at least one proportion is different).

nodes.title: What is the population regression equation?
nodes.I: y = alpha + betax + epsilon (where beta is the true slope).

nodes.title: What is the Null Hypothesis for a slope test?
nodes.I: H0: beta = 0 (implies no linear relationship).

nodes.title: How do you find degrees of freedom for regression inference?
nodes.I: df = n - 2.

nodes.title: What is the formula for the t-interval for slope?
How do you check the "Normal Residuals" condition?
nodes.K: Look at a histogram or Normal Probability Plot of the residuals and check for normality.
nodes.I: Look at a histogram or Normal Probability Plot of the residuals and check for normality.

nodes.title: Where is the sample slope located in a computer output table?
nodes.I: The coefficient in the row for the explanatory (X) variable.

nodes.title: What does "S" represent in regression computer output?
nodes.I: The standard deviation of the residuals.

nodes.title: What is the calculator command for slope inference?
nodes.I: LinRegTTest.

nodes.title: Difference between "accuracy" and "precision"?
nodes.I: Accuracy is about bias (hitting the center); precision is about variability (tight clusters).

nodes.title: If you switch X and Y, what happens to r?
nodes.I: Nothing. r remains the same.

nodes.title: What is a "Lurking Variable"?
nodes.I: An unmeasured variable that influences the relationship between the variables being studied.

nodes.title: What is the "Power" of a test?
nodes.I: 1 - P(Type II Error).

nodes.title: How do you decrease the probability of a Type II Error?
nodes.I: Increase sample size, increase alpha, or increase the effect size.

nodes.title: What is a "Density Curve"?
nodes.I: A curve that is always on or above the axis and has a total area of 1.

nodes.title: What is a "Random Phenomenon"?
nodes.I: Outcomes are uncertain in the short term but have a predictable distribution in the long run.

nodes.title: What is the probability of a sure event?
What is a "Statistic of Interest"?
nodes.I: The sample value used to estimate the parameter.

nodes.title: What is "Standard Error of the Mean"?
nodes.I: s-x / sqrt(n).

nodes.title: What is the significance level (alpha)?
nodes.I: The threshold for rejecting the null; also the probability of a Type I error.

nodes.title: What does "Two-Sided" Ha mean?
nodes.K: Testing if a parameter is "different from" (not equal to) a value.
nodes.I: Testing if a parameter is "different from" (not equal to) a value.

nodes.title: Why do we randomize in an experiment?
nodes.I: To balance confounding variables across treatment groups.

nodes.title: Why use replication?
nodes.I: To ensure the results are consistent and not just a fluke in one small group.

nodes.title: Definition of "Statistically Significant"?
nodes.I: The probability of the result occurring by chance is very small (usually < 0.05).

nodes.title: What is the Law of Large Numbers?
nodes.F: As n increases, the sample mean approaches the true population mean.
nodes.I: As n increases, the sample mean approaches the true population mean.

nodes.title: How do you identify a 'Resistant' statistic?
nodes.I: It is not strongly affected by outliers (Median, IQR).

nodes.title: Define Type I Error in context.
nodes.I: Concluding the effect exists when it actually does not.

nodes.title: How does increasing n affect Power?
nodes.I: It increases Power by reducing variability.

nodes.title: What is an 'Experimental Unit'?
nodes.I: The smallest collection of individuals to which treatments are applied.

nodes.title: What is 'Extrapolation'?
nodes.F: Predicting y for x-values outside the observed data range; it is unreliable.
nodes.I: Predicting y for x-values outside the observed data range; it is unreliable.

nodes.title: What is the null for a Chi-Square GOF test?
nodes.F: H0: The specified distribution is correct.
nodes.I: H0: The specified distribution is correct.

nodes.title: What is a 'Lurking Variable'?
nodes.I: A variable not included in the study that affects the relationship between variables.

nodes.title: How do you calculate degrees of freedom for Chi-Square Independence?
Define 'Alpha' (alpha).
nodes.F: The significance level; the threshold for rejecting H0.
nodes.I: The significance level; the threshold for rejecting H0.

nodes.title: What is the 'Margin of Error'?
nodes.I: The maximum expected difference between the sample result and the true parameter.

nodes.title: What is a 'Sampling Frame'?
nodes.I: The list of individuals from which a sample is drawn.

nodes.title: Define 'Placebo Effect'.
nodes.I: Subjects showing improvement simply because they believe they are being treated.

nodes.title: Define 'Stratified Random Sample'.
nodes.I: Dividing the population into strata and taking an SRS from each.

nodes.title: What is 'Non-response Bias'?
nodes.I: When people chosen for a survey cannot be reached or refuse to participate.

nodes.title: Define 'Skewed Right'.
nodes.I: Tail is on the right; Mean > Median.

nodes.title: What is the 'Empirical Rule'?
nodes.K: 68-95-99.7% of data in a Normal distribution falls within 1, 2, and 3 SDs.
nodes.I: 68-95-99.7% of data in a Normal distribution falls within 1, 2, and 3 SDs.

nodes.title: Define 'Residual'.
nodes.I: Actual value - Predicted value (y - y-hat).

nodes.title: What is 'Statistically Significant'?
nodes.F: A result so extreme it is unlikely to have occurred by chance (P < alpha).
nodes.I: A result so extreme it is unlikely to have occurred by chance (P < alpha).

nodes.title: What is the 'Union' of two events?
nodes.F: Either event or both occurring (A or B).
nodes.I: Either event or both occurring (A or B).

nodes.title: Define 'Conditional Probability'.
nodes.I: The probability of an event occurring given that another has already occurred.

nodes.title: What is a 'Geometric Setting'?
nodes.I: BITS: Binary, Independent, Trials until first success, Success probability constant.

nodes.title: What is the 'Central Limit Theorem'?
nodes.F: The sampling distribution of the mean becomes Normal as n increases (n >= 30).
nodes.K: The sampling distribution of the mean becomes Normal as n increases (n >= 30).
nodes.I: The sampling distribution of the mean becomes Normal as n increases (n >= 30).

nodes.title: What is 'Point Estimate'?
nodes.I: A single value from a sample used to estimate a population parameter.

nodes.title: What is a 'Two-sided Test'?
nodes.F: A test where Ha is "not equal to," looking for effects in both directions.
nodes.K: A test where Ha is "not equal to," looking for effects in both directions.
nodes.I: A test where Ha is "not equal to," looking for effects in both directions.

nodes.title: Define 'Bias'.
nodes.I: Systematic error in a study that favors certain outcomes over others.

nodes.title: Define 'Extrapolation'.
nodes.I: Using a regression line to predict values far outside the range of the data.

nodes.title: Define 'Margin of Error'.
nodes.I: The range of values above and below a sample statistic that likely contains the true parameter.

nodes.title: Define 'P-value'.
nodes.I: The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the observed results, assuming the null is true.

nodes.title: Define 'Statistically Significant'.
nodes.I: When an observed effect is so large that it would rarely occur by chance.

nodes.title: Define 'Type II Error'.
nodes.I: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false (False Negative).

nodes.title: Descriptive Statistics Formulas
nodes.F: Mean: x-bar = (Sum xi)/(n). Variance: s^2 = \fracSum (xi - x-bar)^2n-1. Standard Deviation: s = sqrt(s^2). LSRL: y-hat = a + bx. Slope: b = r (sy)/(sx). Y-int: a = y-bar - bx-bar.
nodes.I: Mean: x-bar = (Sum xi)/(n). Variance: s^2 = \fracSum (xi - x-bar)^2n-1. Standard Deviation: s = sqrt(s^2). LSRL: y-hat = a + bx. Slope: b = r (sy)/(sx). Y-int: a = y-bar - bx-bar.

nodes.title: Probability Distribution Formulas (Binomial/Geometric)
nodes.F: Binomial: P(X=k) = \binomnk p^k (1-p)^n-k. Mean: mu = np. SD: sigma = sqrt(np(1-p)). Geometric: P(X=k) = (1-p)^k-1 p. Mean: mu = 1/p. SD: sigma = sqrt(1-p)/p.
nodes.K: Binomial: P(X=k) = \binomnk p^k (1-p)^n-k. Mean: mu = np. SD: sigma = sqrt(np(1-p)). Geometric: P(X=k) = (1-p)^k-1 p. Mean: mu = 1/p. SD: sigma = sqrt(1-p)/p.
nodes.I: Binomial: P(X=k) = \binomnk p^k (1-p)^n-k. Mean: mu = np. SD: sigma = sqrt(np(1-p)). Geometric: P(X=k) = (1-p)^k-1 p. Mean: mu = 1/p. SD: sigma = sqrt(1-p)/p.

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: The 10% Condition
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Never use the 10% condition (n <= 0.10N) if you are analyzing a randomized experiment. It only applies when sampling *without replacement* from a broader population.

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: Large Counts vs. Normal/Large Sample
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Proportions use the Large Counts condition (np >= 10, n(1-p) >= 10). Means use the Normal/Large Sample condition (n >= 30 or Normal population). Do not mix these up on paper.

nodes.title: FRQ T-Test Condition Check
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If n < 30 and the population is not stated as Normal, you MUST draw a quick dotplot or stemplot of the sample data on your paper and state: "The graph shows no strong skew or clear outliers, so the t-procedure is appropriate."

nodes.title: Interpreting a P-value (FRQ Standard)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "Assuming the null hypothesis is true [context], there is a [P-value] probability of getting a sample statistic as extreme or more extreme than the one observed, strictly by chance."

nodes.title: Interpreting Confidence Level (FRQ Standard)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "If we were to select many, many random samples of size [n] and construct a [C%] confidence interval from each, about [C%] of these intervals would capture the true [parameter in context]."

nodes.title: Chi-Square GOF Hypotheses
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: H0: The specified distribution of [variable] is correct. Ha: The specified distribution of [variable] is not correct. Always write these in words, never in symbols.

nodes.title: Chi-Square Independence Hypotheses
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: H0: There is no association between [Variable 1] and [Variable 2]. Ha: There is an association between [Variable 1] and [Variable 2].

nodes.title: Chi-Square Homogeneity Hypotheses
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: H0: The distribution of [Variable] is the same for [Population 1] and [Population 2]. Ha: The distribution of [Variable] is different for [Population 1] and [Population 2].

nodes.title: Regression Slope Null Hypothesis
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: H0: beta = 0. In words: "There is no true linear relationship between [X variable] and [Y variable]."

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: Chi-Square Expected Counts
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: The rubric requires you to show at least the first two and the last calculation for the expected counts, OR explicitly state the formula used before writing out the matrix values.

nodes.title: Type I Error Context
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "We find convincing evidence that [Alternative Hypothesis], when in reality [Null Hypothesis is true]." You MUST include the real-world consequence of this error to get full credit.

nodes.title: Type II Error Context
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "We fail to find convincing evidence that [Alternative Hypothesis], when in reality [Alternative Hypothesis is actually true]." Include the consequence.

nodes.title: Increasing Power
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: In an FRQ, if asked how to increase the power of a test, state: "Increase the sample size (n) or increase the significance level (alpha)."

nodes.title: Experimental Design FRQ
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If asked to design an experiment, explicitly list: 1) The completely randomized pool, 2) The random assignment mechanism, 3) The specific treatments, 4) The response variable being compared.

nodes.title: Blocking Justification
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "We blocked by [Variable] because it is known to affect the [Response Variable]. Blocking reduces the variation within groups, making it easier to see the true effect of the treatments."

nodes.title: Matched Pairs Justification
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "This is a matched pairs design because each subject received both treatments in a randomized order, which controls for individual variability."

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: Standard Error vs Standard Deviation
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If an FRQ asks for the meaning of "SE Coef" in a regression table, it is the *Standard Error of the Slope*: "If we repeated this study many times, the sample slope would typically vary from the true population slope by [SE Coef value]."

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: S in Regression Output
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "S" is the standard deviation of the residuals. "The actual [Y variable] typically varies by [S value] away from the value predicted by the least-squares regression line."

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: The Y-Intercept Meaning
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Only interpret the y-intercept if x=0 is a plausible value. Otherwise, state: "The y-intercept has no practical meaning in this context because an x-value of 0 is impossible/far outside the data range."

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: Combining Standard Deviations
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: You can only combine variances (sigma^2), NEVER standard deviations directly. Square them, add them, then take the square root. You can only do this if the variables are independent.

nodes.title: Inverse T-Distribution
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: [2nd] > VARS > 4:invT(area, df). Use this to find the critical t^* value for confidence intervals manually.

nodes.title: Checking Independence (Probability)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: To prove independence on an FRQ, mathematically show that P(A|B) = P(A). If the two numbers are equal, they are independent.

nodes.title: Mutually Exclusive Check
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Mathematically show that P(A AND B) = 0. If they share outcomes, they are not mutually exclusive.

nodes.title: Stratified vs Cluster
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Stratified takes *some* from *all* groups. Cluster takes *all* from *some* groups. Use this exact phrasing to distinguish them on FRQs.

nodes.title: Scope of Inference (Selection)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If individuals were randomly selected from a population, you can generalize the results to that entire population.

nodes.title: Scope of Inference (Assignment)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If individuals were randomly assigned to treatments, you can infer cause and effect.

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: "Prove" or "Confirm"
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Never use the words "prove" or "confirm" in statistics. Use "provides convincing evidence" or "suggests."

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: Accepting the Null
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Never say "We accept the null hypothesis." Always say "We fail to reject the null hypothesis."

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: Confounding vs Lurking
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Confounding variables are tied to the explanatory variable and affect the response (experiments). Lurking variables are unmeasured variables driving the relationship (observational studies).

nodes.title: Identifying the Parameter
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: mu is a mean, p is a proportion, beta is a slope. Make sure you use the correct Greek letter in your hypotheses.

nodes.title: Two-Sample vs Matched Pairs
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If there are two distinct groups of different people, it is two-sample. If the same people do both tasks, or they are explicitly paired up by a trait, it is matched pairs.

nodes.title: FRQ Trap: Normalizing a List
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If asked to compare two scores from different Normal distributions, calculate the Z-score for both.

nodes.title: Z-score Interpretation
nodes.I: N/A

nodes.title: Percentile Interpretation
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "[Percentile]% of the [population/individuals] had a [variable] at or below [value]."

nodes.title: Extrapolation Danger
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "We cannot trust the prediction for x = [value] because it is far outside the interval of x-values used to create the regression line."

nodes.title: Residual Interpretation
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: "The actual [Y variable] was [Residual value] [higher/lower] than predicted by the regression line."

nodes.title: Transforming Data (Power Model)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If a scatterplot is curved, highlight L3, type log(L1). Highlight L4, type log(L2). Run LinReg on L3 and L4 to straighten it.

nodes.title: Reading a Transformed Equation
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If the equation is \log(y-hat) = a + b(x), you must calculate 10^answer to get the final predicted y value.

nodes.title: Degrees of Freedom (Unpooled T-Test)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Always use the calculator's complex fractional df for 2-sample t-tests, but write down the df on your paper so graders know where your P-value came from.

nodes.title: Chi-Square Cell Contribution
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: The cell with the largest ((O-E)^2)/(E) contributed the most to the Chi-Square statistic. Identify this if asked "which category differed most from expected."

nodes.title: Calculator Trap (Syntax)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Never write "normalcdf" or "tcdf" on your paper as your primary work. Write the formula, then use the calculator to get the answer.

nodes.title: Calculator Trap (Labels)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If you use calculator speak as a backup, define the inputs: "normalcdf(lower=[val], upper=[val], mean=[val], sd=[val])."

nodes.title: Law of Large Numbers Application
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Used to explain why insurance companies or casinos make money in the long run, despite short-term variability.

nodes.title: Expected Value vs Actual
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Never say the expected value *will* happen. Say it is the *long-run average*.

nodes.title: Confidence Interval vs Level
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: The interval is the specific range of numbers. The level is the methodology's success rate.

nodes.title: Overlapping Confidence Intervals
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Do not use overlapping confidence intervals to test for a difference between two groups. Run a proper 2-sample test instead.

nodes.title: Margin of Error Components
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Margin of error only accounts for sampling variability. It does *not* account for bias, undercoverage, or non-response.

nodes.title: Simulations in FRQs
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: 1) Assign digits to outcomes. 2) State how to read digits. 3) State what to ignore (repeats). 4) State when to stop a trial. 5) State what to record.

nodes.title: Robustness
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: T-tests are robust to slight departures from Normality, especially if the sample size is large.

nodes.title: The Golden Rule of AP Stats
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: ALWAYS INCLUDE CONTEXT. A perfect mathematical answer with no words attached will score a Partial (P) or Incorrect (I).

nodes.title: DiagnosticOn (The r-Value fix)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If you don't see r or r^2 after running LinReg, go to [2nd] > 0 (CATALOG) > scroll to DiagnosticOn > ENTER.

nodes.title: List Math (Manual Deviations)
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Highlight the name of L2. Type (L1 - mean(L1))^2 to quickly calculate squared deviations for every point.

nodes.title: Table View for Probabilities
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: If you store a Binomial formula in Y1, you can press [2nd] > GRAPH (TABLE) to see all probabilities for X=1, 2, 3... at once.

nodes.title: Simulation Speed-Up
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: Use randIntNoRep(1, n) if your calculator supports it (CE models only). It automatically prevents duplicates in your sample.

nodes.title: Matrix Expected Counts
nodes.I: N/A
nodes.T: After a Chi-Square test, the expected counts are stored in [B]. View them via MATRIX > [B].

nodes.title: Describing a Univariate Distribution (Unit 1)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Students list the stats but forget context or skip a required element. 
The Rule: You must use SOCS (Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread) AND include the context (units/variable name).
 Template: "The distribution of [variable name/context] is [Shape: roughly symmetric / right-skewed / left-skewed]. There [are / are no] apparent outliers [list them if they exist]. The center of the distribution is a [median/mean] of [value] [units], and the spread is best described by an [IQR / Standard Deviation] of [value] [units]."
 FRQ Hack: If it's skewed, specifically name the Median and IQR. If it's symmetric, specifically name the Mean and Standard Deviation.

nodes.title: Comparing Two Distributions (Unit 1)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Students describe both distributions perfectly but fail to actually compare them.
The Rule: You must use explicit comparison words (greater than, less than, roughly equal to) for the Center and the Spread.
 Template: "Both distributions of [context] are [Shape]. However, Group A has a noticeably higher center (Median = [value]) than Group B (Median = [value]). Group A also has a larger spread, with an IQR of [value] compared to Group B's IQR of [value]. Group A contains an outlier at [value], while Group B has no apparent outliers."

nodes.title: Interpreting the LSRL Slope and Y-Intercept (Unit 2)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Using deterministic language (saying "it will increase" instead of "it is predicted to increase").
The Rule: Always use non-probabilistic, predictive language and include units for both X and Y.
 Slope Template: "For every 1 [unit of X] increase in [Explanatory Variable], the [Response Variable] is predicted to [increase/decrease] by [Slope Value] [units of Y]."
 Y-Intercept Template: "If the [Explanatory Variable] is 0 [units of X], the predicted [Response Variable] is [Y-int Value] [units of Y]." (Add a sentence stating if this makes sense in reality, as extrapolating to 0 is often impossible).

nodes.title: Explaining Random Assignment (Unit 3)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Saying "use a random number generator" without explaining exactly how the numbers are assigned and how repeats are handled.
The Rule: You must explain the mechanism so clearly that someone with no statistical knowledge could execute it. 
 The "Hat Trick" Template (Bulletproof for FRQs): "Write the names of all [total number] subjects on identically sized slips of paper. Place them into a hat and mix thoroughly. Draw [number] slips without replacement. These subjects will be assigned to [Treatment 1]. The remaining subjects in the hat will be assigned to [Treatment 2]."

nodes.title: Binomial Probability Calculations (Unit 4)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Just writing "binomcdf(10, 0.5, 4) = 0.377" will get you zero credit for work shown.
The Rule: You must define the distribution, state the parameters, and show the formula setup before writing the calculator output.
 Template: 1. Define: "Let X = the number of [successes in context]." 2. Parameters: "X has a binomial distribution with n = [trials] and p = [probability]." 3. Formula setup: "P(X = k) = \binomnk p^k (1-p)^n-k" 4. Execution: "P(X = 3) = \binom103 (0.5)^3 (0.5)^7 = 0.117" (You can use the calculator to get the 0.117, but you must write the formula).

nodes.title: Expected Value / Mean of a Discrete Random Variable (Unit 4)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Failing to show the summation process.
The Rule: Show at least the first two and the last term of the multiplication string to prove you understand the mechanics, even if you did it in L1/L2.
 Template: 1. "The expected value of [context] is calculated by mux = Sum xi P(xi)." 2. "mux = (Value1 \times Prob1) + (Value2 \times Prob2) + ... + (Valuen \times Probn)" 3. "mux = [Final Answer] [Units]." 4. Interpretation: "If we randomly select many, many [subjects], we expect the average [variable] to be approximately [Final Answer]."

nodes.title: The PANIC Template (Confidence Intervals)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Skipping conditions or misinterpreting the final interval.
The Rule: You must hit all 5 parts exactly.
 P: Parameter: Define the population parameter. "Let p be the true proportion of all [population] who [context]."
 A: Assumptions/Conditions: Verify Random, 10% Rule (n <= 0.10N), and Normal/Large Counts (np-hat >= 10, n(1-p-hat) >= 10 or n >= 30).
 N: Name the Interval: State the procedure. "One-sample z-interval for a proportion."
 I: Interval Calculation: Formula and execution. "Stat +/- (Crit) \times (SE)" -> "0.65 +/- 1.96 \times 0.047 = (0.558, 0.742)"
 C: Conclusion: "We are [95%] confident that the true [parameter] is between [low] and [high]."

nodes.title: The PHANTOMS Template (Hypothesis Tests)
nodes.I:
The Trap: Forgetting to explicitly reject or fail to reject before writing the context conclusion.
The Rule: Follow the 8-step process.
 P: Parameter: "Let mu be the true mean [context]."
 H: Hypotheses: "H0: mu = mu0 vs Ha: mu > mu0."
 A: Assumptions/Conditions: (Same as PANIC).
 N: Name the Test: "One-sample t-test for a mean."
 T: Test Statistic: "t = \fracx-bar - mu0s/sqrt(n) = 2.45."
 O: Obtain P-value: "P-value = 0.007."
 M: Make Decision: "Since P-value (0.007) < alpha (0.05), we reject the null hypothesis."
 S: State Conclusion: "There is convincing evidence that the true mean [context] is [greater than/less than/different from] [value]."

nodes.title: FRQ Action Verbs (Low-Stakes)
nodes.I:
Identify/Indicate/State: Just name the value, term, or concept. Action: No explanation needed.
 Determine: Arrive at an answer through calculation or logic. Action: Show the path (numbers used), but no paragraph justification needed.
 Label/Plot: Physical actions on a graph. Action: Ensure units and scales are clear.

nodes.title: FRQ Action Verbs (Mid-Stakes)
nodes.I:
Calculate: Perform mathematical steps. Action: Must show the formula and the substitution.
 Describe: Provide relevant characteristics. Action: Use SOCS (Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread) with context.
 Construct/Draw: Create a visual model. Action: Must be consistent with the data (e.g., 1.5IQR rule for boxplots).

nodes.title: FRQ Action Verbs (High-Stakes)
nodes.I:
Explain: Show cause and effect. Action: Use "Because" (e.g., "Because p-value < alpha, we reject...").
 Compare: Find similarities and differences. Action: Use comparison words (higher, lower, similar) to link both groups in one sentence.
 Justify: Defend a claim with evidence. Action: Link specific data to a specific statistical rule.
 Verify: Confirm conditions are met. Action: Show the math for the condition check (e.g., np >= 10).

nodes.title: AP Statistics Task Verb Tutorials
nodes.I:
Calculate: Perform mathematical steps. Action: Show the formula, substitute the numbers, and include units. Do not just write the final number.
 Compare: Explain similarities/differences. Action: Link both groups in one sentence using words like "greater than" or "similar to."
 Describe: Provide relevant characteristics. Action: For distributions, use SOCS (Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread) with context.
 Explain: Show cause and effect. Action: Use a "Because" statement to link evidence to the outcome.
 Identify: State a value/term. Action: Name it directly. No explanation needed.
 Interpret: Relate results to context. Action: Use the variable names and units from the problem.
 Justify: Defend a claim. Action: Use statistical evidence (p-values, conditions) to support why the conclusion is valid.
 The "I CAN" Framework: 1. Identify the test. 2. Check conditions. 3. Analyze results (math). 4. Narrate conclusion (context).

nodes.title: Critical Values (Z* and T*) Table
nodes.I:
Z-Star Critical Values: 90%: 1.645 | 95%: 1.96 | 98%: 2.326 | 99%: 2.576. Use `invNorm` on calculator for other levels.
 T-Star Critical Values: Always based on Degrees of Freedom (df = n-1). Use `invT` on calculator. Common levels for df=30: 95%: 2.042 | 99%: 2.750.
 Confidence vs Margin of Error: Increasing confidence increases the width of the interval (makes it less precise). Increasing sample size (n) decreases the width (makes it more precise).

nodes.title: Unit 5: Sampling Distributions (The Bridge)
nodes.I:
The CLT (Central Limit Theorem): Regardless of population shape, the sampling distribution of the mean (x-bar) becomes approximately Normal if n >= 30.
 Law of Large Numbers: As n increases, the sample mean (x-bar) gets closer to the true population mean (mu).
 Unbiased Estimator: A statistic whose mean of its sampling distribution is equal to the true parameter (p-hat = p, x-bar = mu).

nodes.title: FRQ Q6: The Investigative Task
nodes.I:
Strategy: Q6 counts for 25% of your FRQ score. It often introduces a NEW concept you haven't seen. 
 The Trick: Don't panic. Use the definitions provided in the prompt. Part (a) usually asks for something simple to build your confidence. 
 Scoring: Readers give partial credit for "Statistical Integrity." If you get an early part wrong, keep using that number in later parts—you can still get full credit for the later sections!

nodes.title: Unit 10: Comparing Two Populations
nodes.I:
Proportions (z-test): Compare two groups using z = \frac(p-hat1 - p-hat2) - 0sqrt(\hatp)C(1-p-hatC)(1/n1 + 1/n2).
 Means (t-test): Compare two means using t = \frac(x-bar1 - x-bar2) - 0sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2). Use unpooled degrees of freedom.

nodes.title: Unit 11: Chi-Square Tests
nodes.I:
Goodness of Fit: Chi-Square = Sum ((O-E)^2)/(E). Use to see if data fits a claimed distribution. df = categories - 1.
 Homogeneity/Independence: Use a matrix to test if distributions are the same across populations or if two variables are associated. df = (r-1)(c-1).

nodes.title: Unit 12: Inference for Regression
nodes.I:
Conditions (LINER): Linear, Independent, Normal, Equal Variance, Random.
 Testing Slope: t = (b - 0)/(SEb). df = n - 2.

nodes.title: TPS 5e Master Summary (Chapters 1-12)
nodes.I:
Chapter 1 Summary: Describe distributions using SOCS (Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread). Use histograms for large datasets and boxplots for outliers.
 Chapter 2 Summary: Normal distributions follow the 68-95-99.7 rule. Standardize with z = (x - mu)/sigma.
 Chapter 3 Summary: r measures linear strength. r^2 is the % of variation in y explained by x. Interpret the slope as the predicted change.
 Chapter 4 Summary: Random sampling reduces bias. Random assignment allows for cause-and-effect conclusions.
 Chapter 5 Summary: Probability rules (P(A OR B) and P(A|B)). Independence check: P(A|B) = P(A).
 Chapter 6 Summary: Random variables. Mean of X+Y = mux + muy. Variance of X+Y = sigmax^2 + sigmay^2 (if independent).
 Chapter 7 Summary: Sampling distributions. The CLT ensures normality for n \ge 30.
 Chapter 8 Summary: Confidence Intervals. Margin of Error = (Critical Value)  (Standard Error).
 Chapter 9 Summary: Significance Tests. P-value is the probability of results as extreme as observed, assuming H0 is true.
 Chapter 10 Summary: Comparing two groups. Two-sample t-test is for means; two-proportion z-test is for proportions.
 Chapter 11 Summary: Chi-Square. Expected counts must be \ge 5.
 Chapter 12 Summary: Regression inference. Check for no pattern in residuals for linearity.

nodes.title: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
Variable Types: Categorical (counts/percents) vs. Quantitative (measurable values).
 Displaying Categorical: Bar charts (counts) and Pie charts (percents). Never use these for quantitative data.
 Displaying Quantitative: Dotplots (small n), Stemplots (small n, preserves data), Histograms (large n, groups data), Boxplots (highlights outliers).
 SOCS - Shape: Symmetric, Left-Skewed (tail on left, mean < median), Right-Skewed (tail on right, mean > median), Unimodal (one peak), Bimodal (two peaks).
 SOCS - Outliers: The 1.5IQR Rule: Q1 - 1.5(IQR) and Q3 + 1.5(IQR). Any point outside this range is an outlier.
 SOCS - Center: Use Median for skewed data (resistant). Use Mean for symmetric data.
 SOCS - Spread: Use IQR for skewed data. Use Standard Deviation for symmetric data.
 Standard Deviation Meaning: The typical distance a data point is from the mean.
 Comparing Distributions: You MUST use comparison words (greater, smaller, similar) and mention both groups in every sentence.

nodes.title: Unit 2: Modeling Distributions (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
Z-Score Meaning: The number of standard deviations a value is above or below the mean.
 Density Curves: Area under the curve is always 1. The median is the 50th percentile.
 Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7): Applies ONLY to Normal distributions. 68% in 1 SD, 95% in 2 SD, 99.7% in 3 SD.
 Assessing Normality: 1. Check for symmetry in a histogram/boxplot. 2. Verify the 68-95-99.7 rule. 3. Normal Probability Plot (NPP): If the plot is linear, the data is Normal.

nodes.title: Unit 3: Two-Variable Quantitative Data (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
Scatterplots: Describe Direction (+/-), Form (Linear/Curved), Strength (Weak/Moderate/Strong).
 Correlation (r): Measures strength/direction of linear relationship. -1 to 1. Not resistant to outliers.
 LSRL Equation: y-hat = a + bx. y-hat is the predicted value.
 Slope (b) Interpretation: For every 1 unit increase in x, the y-variable is predicted to increase/decrease by [b] units.
 Y-Intercept (a) Interpretation: When x=0, the predicted value of y is [a]. (Often has no practical meaning).
 Residuals: y - y-hat (Actual - Predicted). Positive residual = underprediction. Negative = overprediction.
 Residual Plots: If there is NO PATTERN, a linear model is appropriate. If there is a curve, a linear model is NOT appropriate.
 Coefficient of Determination (r^2): [r^2]% of the variation in [y-variable] is accounted for by the linear relationship with [x-variable].
 Standard Deviation of Residuals (s): The typical distance between the actual y-values and the predicted y-values.

nodes.title: Unit 4: Collecting Data (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
Sampling Methods: SRS (every group has equal chance), Stratified (split by trait, sample some from all), Cluster (split by location, sample all from some), Systematic (every kth individual).
 Bias Types: Voluntary Response (only loud voices), Convenience (easiest to reach), Undercoverage (missing groups), Nonresponse (people won't answer), Response Bias (lying/wording).
 Observational Study: No treatment imposed. Can show association, NOT causation.
 Experiment: Treatment imposed. Random assignment allows for causation.
 Key Principles of Design: 1. Comparison (at least 2 groups). 2. Random Assignment (balances variables). 3. Control (reduces confounding). 4. Replication (many subjects).
 Confounding Variable: An outside variable that affects the response and is tied to the treatment, making it impossible to tell which caused the result.
 Blocking: Grouping subjects by a known variable before assigning treatments to reduce variation. "Block what you can, randomize what you cannot."
 Matched Pairs: Each subject does both treatments, or subjects are paired by a specific trait (twins, height) to control for individual differences.

nodes.title: Unit 5: Probability (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
General Rules: 1. Probabilities are 0 to 1. 2. Sum of all outcomes = 1. 3. Complement: P(A^c) = 1 - P(A).
 Mutually Exclusive: Events cannot happen at same time. P(A AND B) = 0.
 Addition Rule (OR): P(A OR B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A AND B).
 Multiplication Rule (AND): P(A AND B) = P(A) \times P(B|A).
 Independence Check: Events are independent if P(A|B) = P(A) or P(B|A) = P(B).
 Tree Diagrams: Use for conditional probability with multiple steps. Multiply along branches to find the probability of a specific path.
 Venn Diagrams: Use for "At least one" or "Neither" problems. Always start from the middle intersection and work outward.

nodes.title: Unit 6: Random Variables (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
Discrete RV: List of outcomes with associated probabilities. Mean (Expected Value): E(X) = Sum xi P(xi).
 Standard Deviation (Discrete): sigma = sqrt(Sum (xi - mux)^2 P(xi)).
 Continuous RV: Described by a density curve (area = 1). Use `normalcdf` for probabilities.
 Transforming RVs: 1. Adding a constant: Changes Mean, but NOT Spread (SD/IQR/Range). 2. Multiplying a constant: Changes BOTH Mean and Spread.
 Combining RVs: 1. E(X +/- Y) = E(X) +/- E(Y). 2. VAR(X +/- Y) = VAR(X) + VAR(Y) (MUST be independent). ALWAYS ADD VARIANCES, NEVER SUBTRACT.
 Binomial Distribution (BINS): Binary (Success/Fail), Independent, Number of trials fixed, Success probability constant.
 Binomial Formulas: Mean = np. SD = sqrt(np(1-p)).
 Geometric Distribution (BITS): Binary, Independent, Trials until first success, Success probability constant.
 Geometric Formulas: Mean = 1/p. SD = sqrt(1-p)/p.

nodes.title: Unit 7: Sampling Distributions (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
Parameter vs Statistic: Parameter = Population (mu, p). Statistic = Sample (x-bar, p-hat).
 Sampling Variability: The concept that different random samples produce different statistics.
 Unbiased Estimator: A statistic whose mean of its sampling distribution equals the true parameter.
 Standard Error (SE): The estimated standard deviation of a sampling distribution.
 Sampling Distribution of Proportion (p-hat): Mean = p. SD = sqrt(p(1-p)/n). Condition: Normal if np \ge 10 and n(1-p) \ge 10.
 Sampling Distribution of Mean (x-bar): Mean = mu. SD = sigma/sqrt(n).
 Central Limit Theorem (CLT): If n \ge 30, the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately Normal regardless of the population shape.
 Rule for SD Formulas: You must check the 10% condition (n \le 0.10N) before using the Standard Deviation formulas for sampling distributions.

nodes.title: Unit 8: Confidence Intervals for Proportions (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
The Goal: Estimate the true population proportion (p).
 PANIC - Parameter: "Let p be the true proportion of [context]."
 PANIC - Assumptions: 1. Random (stated). 2. 10% Rule (n \le 0.10N). 3. Large Counts (np \ge 10 and n(1-p) \ge 10).
 PANIC - Name: "One-sample z-interval for a proportion."
 PANIC - Interval: p-hat +/- z^ sqrt(\hatp)(1-p-hat)/n.
 Critical Value (z): 90%: 1.645 | 95%: 1.96 | 99%: 2.576.
 PANIC - Conclusion: "We are [C%] confident that the true proportion of [context] is between [low] and [high]."
 Interpretation of Confidence Level: "If we were to take many, many random samples and construct intervals, about [C%] of them would capture the true proportion."

nodes.title: Unit 9: Significance Tests for Proportions (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
The Goal: Test a claim about a population proportion.
 PHANTOMS - Parameter: "Let p be the true proportion..."
 PHANTOMS - Hypotheses: H0: p = p0 vs Ha: p > / < / != p0.
 PHANTOMS - Assumptions: (Same as PANIC).
 PHANTOMS - Name: "One-sample z-test for a proportion."
 PHANTOMS - Test Statistic: z = \fracp-hat - p0sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n).
 PHANTOMS - Obtain P-value: Use `1-PropZTest` or `normalcdf`.
 PHANTOMS - Make Decision: "Since P-value < alpha, we reject the null."
 PHANTOMS - State Conclusion: "There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of [context] is [Ha description]."

nodes.title: Units 10 & 11: Inference for Means (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
The Goal: Estimate or test the true population mean (mu).
 The T-Distribution: Use when sigma is unknown. Wider tails than Normal. Degrees of Freedom (df = n-1).
 Assumptions for Means: 1. Random. 2. 10% Rule. 3. Normal/Large Sample: Either population is Normal, OR n \ge 30 (CLT), OR a sample graph shows no strong skew/outliers.
 Confidence Interval (T-Interval): x-bar +/- t^ (s/sqrt(n)).
 Significance Test (T-Test): t = \fracx-bar - mu0s/sqrt(n).
 Two-Sample Inference: Use when comparing two separate groups. df is calculated by the calculator (unpooled).
 Matched Pairs Inference: Calculate the DIFFERENCES (L1 - L2) first. Run a 1-sample t-procedure on the list of differences. H0: mudiff = 0.

nodes.title: Unit 11: Chi-Square Tests (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
Goodness of Fit (GOF): One population, one variable. Tests if data follows a specific distribution. df = cats - 1.
 Test of Independence: One population, two variables. Tests for an association. df = (r-1)(c-1).
 Test of Homogeneity: Two+ populations, one variable. Tests if distributions are identical. df = (r-1)(c-1).
 Assumptions: 1. Random. 2. 10% Rule. 3. Large Counts (ALL EXPECTED COUNTS MUST BE \ge 5).
 Chi-Square Calculation: Chi-Square = Sum ((O-E)^2)/(E).

nodes.title: Unit 12: Inference for Regression (Deep Dive)
nodes.I:
LINER Conditions: 1. Linear (Residual plot shows no pattern). 2. Independent (10% rule). 3. Normal (Histogram of residuals is symmetric). 4. Equal Variance (Residual plot has consistent vertical spread). 5. Random (Stated).
 Confidence Interval for Slope (beta): b +/- t^ SEb. df = n-2.
 Significance Test for Slope: H0: beta = 0 (No linear relationship). t = (b - 0)/(SEb).
 Standard Error of the Slope (SEb): The typical distance between the sample slope and the true population slope.

nodes.title: Extended Master Glossary (Part 2 - Advanced Terms)
nodes.I:
Adherence: How closely subjects follow the experimental protocol.
 Back-to-back Stemplot: Comparing two groups using a shared vertical stem.
 Bimodal: A distribution with two distinct peaks (modes).
 Bivariate Data: Data involving two variables (x and y).
 Blocking Factor: The variable used to group subjects before randomization.
 Bootstrap: Re-sampling with replacement to estimate a sampling distribution.
 Categorical Data: Qualitative data that labels individuals into groups.
 Central Limit Theorem: The rule that means of large samples follow a Normal curve.
 Coefficient of Determination: r-squared. % of variation explained by the model.
 Conditional Distribution: The distribution of one variable given a specific value of another.
 Confounding Variable: A variable that creates a fake association between two others.
 Continuity Correction: Adjusting a discrete distribution to fit a continuous model.
 Control Group: The group that receives a placebo or no treatment.
 Critical Value: The number of standard errors needed for a specific confidence level.
 Cumulative Relative Frequency: The sum of relative frequencies up to a certain point.
 Degrees of Freedom: Values used to adjust for sample size in t-tests and chi-square.
 Discrete Random Variable: A variable with a finite or countable number of outcomes.
 Double-Blind: Neither the subjects nor the researchers know who got which treatment.
 Efficiency: A measure of how quickly an estimator approaches the true parameter.
 Expected Count: The number of occurrences predicted by a null hypothesis.
 Experimental Units: The individuals or objects assigned to treatments.
 Explanatory Variable: The variable (x) used to predict the response.
 Extrapolation: Predicting values far outside the observed data range.
 False Positive: A Type I error in a medical or legal context.
 Five-Number Summary: Min, Q1, Median, Q3, Max.
 Homogeneity: Testing if different populations have the same distribution.
 Influential Point: A data point that significantly changes the slope of a regression line.
 Joint Frequency: The count of individuals in a specific category of a two-way table.
 Law of Large Numbers: The long-run average approaches the true average.
 Least-Squares Regression: The line that makes the sum of squared residuals smallest.
 Level of Significance: Alpha. The cutoff for rejecting the null.
 Lurking Variable: A variable NOT included in the study that affects results.
 Marginal Distribution: The distribution of one variable in a two-way table.
 Matched Pairs Design: Pairing subjects by a trait to reduce variation.
 Mean Absolute Deviation: The average distance of data points from the mean.
 Multistage Sampling: Combining multiple sampling methods (e.g. Cluster then SRS).
 Non-Resistant Measure: A statistic easily changed by outliers (Mean, SD, Range).
 Normal Probability Plot: A plot used to check if data is approximately Normal.
 Observational Study: Studying subjects without trying to influence them.
 Outlier: A value more than 1.5IQR away from the nearest quartile.
 P-value: The probability of getting results at least as extreme as observed.
 Parameter: A number that describes the whole population.
 Placebo Effect: When subjects improve just because they think they are treated.
 Population: Every single individual we are interested in.
 Power: 1 - Beta. The probability of rejecting a false null.
 Probability Distribution: A list of all outcomes and their probabilities.
 Random Assignment: The key to showing cause-and-effect in experiments.
 Random Variable: A variable whose value is determined by a random process.
 Regression Line: A line used to model a linear relationship.
 Residual: The vertical distance between a data point and the line.
 Resistant Measure: A statistic NOT affected by outliers (Median, IQR).
 Response Variable: The variable (y) we are trying to measure or predict.
 Robust Procedure: A test that works even if conditions are slightly violated.
 Sampling Bias: When a sample does not accurately represent the population.
 Sampling Distribution: The distribution of all possible sample statistics.
 Standard Deviation: A measure of the typical distance from the mean.
 Standard Error: The estimated standard deviation of a statistic.
 Statistic: A number that describes a specific sample.
 Stratified Random Sample: Splitting by a trait then taking an SRS from each group.
 Systematic Random Sample: Choosing every nth person from a random starting point.
 Test Statistic: A number (z, t, or chi-square) used to find a p-value.
 Two-Way Table: Displays relationship between two categorical variables.
 Type I Error: Saying there is an effect when there isn't.
 Type II Error: Saying there is no effect when there is.
 Undercoverage: Leaving out entire groups from a sample.
 Univariate Data: Data involving only one variable.
 Upper Tail: The right side of a probability distribution.
 Variance: Standard deviation squared. Always add these, never subtract.
 Voluntary Response Bias: When only people with strong opinions join a study.
 Z-score: Standardizing a value into standard deviations.

nodes.title: The Official Formula Sheet Masterclass
nodes.I:
Mean of Sample Mean (muxbar): This is always equal to the population mean (mu). No calculation needed. Use this when defining the center of a sampling distribution.
 SD of Sample Mean (sigmaxbar): sigma / sqrt(n). Use this ONLY if the 10% condition is met. This measures how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample.
 Mean of Sample Proportion (muphat): This is always equal to the population proportion (p). Use this to show that phat is an unbiased estimator.
 SD of Sample Proportion (sigmaphat): sqrt(p(1-p)/n). Use this ONLY if the 10% condition is met. Use phat in place of p for confidence intervals (Standard Error).
 Linear Regression Slope (b1): r  (sy / sx). The slope represents the predicted change in y for every 1 unit increase in x.
 Linear Regression Intercept (b0): ybar - b1xbar. The line always passes through the point (xbar, ybar).
 Probability Addition Rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Subtract the intersection so you don't double count.
 Conditional Probability Rule: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Read as "The probability of A GIVEN B."
 Binomial Mean (mu): n  p. The expected number of successes in n trials.
 Binomial SD (sigma): sqrt(n  p  (1-p)). The typical deviation from the expected number of successes.
 Chi-Square Statistic: Sum of (Observed - Expected)^2 / Expected. A measure of how far your data is from what was predicted by the null.
 Standardized Test Statistic: (Statistic - Parameter) / Standard Error. Tells you how many standard errors the sample is from the null value.

nodes.title: Exhaustive Unit Transcripts (Units 1-9 Deep Content)
nodes.I:
Unit 1 Transcript: Exploring data is about finding patterns. Always start with a picture. For quantitative data, use a histogram or dotplot. Look for SOCS. Shape (skewed?), Outliers (1.5IQR?), Center (median?), Spread (IQR?). If the data is skewed, the mean is pulled toward the tail. The median is resistant, meaning it doesn't move much with outliers. Standard deviation is NOT resistant.
 Unit 2 Transcript: Normal distributions are theoretical models. They are defined by mu and sigma. All Normal curves follow the 68-95-99.7 rule. To find area, standardize to a z-score first. z = (value - mean) / SD. Use normalcdf(lower, upper, mu, sigma) on the TI-84. To find a value from an area, use invNorm(area, mu, sigma).
 Unit 3 Transcript: Bivariate data looks at the relationship between two variables. Direction can be positive or negative. Form is usually linear in AP Stats. Strength is measured by r. If r is close to 1 or -1, it's strong. Residuals are actual y - predicted y. A residual plot with no pattern means a linear model is appropriate.
 Unit 4 Transcript: Sampling is how we get data. Random sampling is a MUST to avoid bias. SRS is the gold standard. Stratified sampling reduces variation by grouping similar individuals. Experiments are different; they impose a treatment. Random assignment is required to show cause-and-effect. Blocking is like stratified sampling but for experiments.
 Unit 5 Transcript: Probability is long-run relative frequency. Simulation is a great way to estimate probability. Use randInt on the TI-84. Independence means knowing one outcome doesn't change the other. Disjoint (mutually exclusive) events cannot be independent because if one happens, the other can't.
 Unit 6 Transcript: Random variables can be discrete or continuous. When adding two independent random variables, you add their means AND you add their variances. Never subtract variances. Standard deviation is the square root of the sum of variances.
 Unit 7 Transcript: Sampling distributions are the heart of inference. The Central Limit Theorem says that if n is at least 30, the distribution of xbar is Normal even if the population isn't. This allows us to use z and t procedures for means.
 Unit 8 Transcript: Confidence intervals estimate parameters. Margin of error depends on the confidence level and the sample size. To decrease MoE, you can either decrease confidence (bad) or increase sample size (good).
 Unit 9 Transcript: Significance tests evaluate claims. P-value is the probability of your sample result (or more extreme) happening by chance if the null is true. Small p-value = reject the null = convincing evidence for the alternative.
 Unit 10 Transcript: Comparing two proportions or two means. For proportions, use a pooled estimate (pc) for the standard error in significance tests. For means, never pool; the TI-84 handles the complex degrees of freedom for you.
 Unit 11 Transcript: Chi-square tests are for categorical data. GOF tests one variable against a distribution. Independence tests two variables in one population. Homogeneity tests one variable across two or more populations.
 Unit 12 Transcript: Linear regression inference tests if there is a linear relationship in the population. H0 is usually that the slope (beta) is zero. Check the residual plot for "no pattern" and "consistent thickness" (equal variance).

nodes.title: Famous Statistical Case Studies (The AP Legend Files)
nodes.I:
The Challenger Disaster Study: In 1986, the Space Shuttle Challenger exploded because of O-ring failure. Engineers had data on O-ring damage at various temperatures but they only looked at flights where damage occurred. By ignoring the "success" data, they missed a clear logistic regression relationship. The lesson: Always look at the full dataset, not just the outliers.
 The 1936 Literary Digest Poll: The magazine polled 2 million people and predicted Alf Landon would beat FDR in a landslide. FDR won 46 states. The problem? They sampled people from phone books and car registrations during the Great Depression. This was selection bias; only the wealthy had phones and cars. This is the ultimate example of why a large sample size doesn't fix a biased sampling method.
 Simpson's Paradox (Berkeley 1973): UC Berkeley was sued for gender bias because men were admitted at a higher rate than women. However, when looking department-by-department, women actually had a HIGHER admission rate in most cases. The paradox occurred because women applied to more competitive departments with lower overall admission rates. Lesson: Lurking variables (choice of major) can reverse the direction of an association.
 The Monty Hall Problem: A game show where you pick one of three doors. One has a car, two have goats. After you pick, the host opens a door with a goat and asks if you want to switch. Math proves switching gives you a 2/3 chance of winning, while staying is only 1/3. This is the classic example of conditional probability being counter-intuitive.
 The Salk Vaccine Trial (1954): The largest medical experiment in history. 1.8 million children. It was a double-blind, placebo-controlled experiment. This setup allowed researchers to definitively prove the vaccine worked by eliminating the placebo effect and researcher bias.

nodes.title: CED Objective Encyclopedia (Units 1-2 Deep Analysis)
nodes.I:
Objective 1.1 - Variable Types: Distinguish between categorical and quantitative. Quantitative variables can be discrete (countable) or continuous (measurable). Categorical variables describe qualities. Note: A zip code is CATEGORICAL even though it's a number because you can't calculate a meaningful average zip code.
 Objective 1.2 - Data Displays: Bar charts and pie charts for categorical. Dotplots, stemplots, and histograms for quantitative. Always check the scale of the axis; a misleading scale can hide skew or exaggerate differences.
 Objective 1.3 - Measuring Center: Mean vs Median. The mean is the balance point. The median is the 50th percentile. In symmetric distributions, they are equal. In skewed distributions, the mean is further out in the tail.
 Objective 1.4 - Measuring Spread: Standard deviation vs IQR. SD measures the typical distance from the mean. IQR measures the spread of the middle half of the data. Use IQR for skewed data because it is resistant to outliers.
 Objective 2.1 - Relative Position: Percentiles and Z-scores. A percentile tells you the % of data at or below your value. A Z-score standardizes the value into standard deviations. z = (x - mu) / sigma.
 Objective 2.2 - Density Curves: A curve that models a distribution. Total area = 1. The area under the curve between two points represents the proportion of data in that range.
 Objective 2.3 - The Normal Distribution: The bell curve. Symmetric, unimodal. Follows the 68-95-99.7 rule. Use normalcdf for probability and invNorm for percentiles. To check for normality, look for a linear pattern in a Normal Probability Plot.

nodes.title: CED Objective Encyclopedia (Units 3-4 Deep Analysis)
nodes.I:
Objective 3.1 - Scatterplots: The primary tool for bivariate data. Always look for Direction, Form, Strength, and Outliers. A strong relationship has points tightly clustered around the line.
 Objective 3.2 - Correlation: r. Measures linear strength. It is not affected by units (e.g. inches to cm) and it makes no distinction between explanatory and response variables.
 Objective 3.3 - Linear Regression: The line of best fit. It minimizes the sum of squared residuals. y-hat = a + bx.
 Objective 3.4 - Residuals: Actual - Predicted. A residual plot checks if the linear model is appropriate. If you see a curve, the linear model is bad.
 Objective 3.5 - Least Squares Regression: Understand that the line MUST pass through the point (x-bar, y-bar). The slope b = r \times (sy / sx).
 Objective 3.6 - Influential Points: A point that, if removed, substantially changes the slope, intercept, or correlation. High-leverage points have extreme x-values.
 Objective 4.1 - Sampling and Surveys: The goal is to generalize to a population. You MUST use a random sampling method to avoid bias.
 Objective 4.2 - Experiments: The goal is to show causation. You MUST use random assignment to treatment groups.
 Objective 4.3 - Blinding: A technique to reduce bias. Single-blind means subjects don't know the treatment. Double-blind means researchers also don't know.
 Objective 4.4 - Confounding: When the effect of the treatment cannot be separated from the effect of an outside variable. Randomization helps prevent this.

nodes.title: CED Objective Encyclopedia (Units 5-6 Deep Analysis)
nodes.I:
Objective 5.1 - Probability Rules: The basics of chance. Complement rule, addition rule for disjoint events, and multiplication rule for independent events.
 Objective 5.2 - Conditional Probability: The probability of an event given another occurred. P(A|B) = P(A AND B) / P(B).
 Objective 5.3 - Independence: Two events are independent if knowing one happened doesn't change the probability of the other. Check P(A|B) = P(A).
 Objective 6.1 - Discrete Random Variables: A list of outcomes and probabilities. The sum of probabilities must be 1. The mean is the expected value.
 Objective 6.2 - Continuous Random Variables: Probability is the area under a density curve. The probability of any single exact value (like exactly 5.000) is 0.
 Objective 6.3 - Binomial Distribution: Fixed trials, independent, constant p, success/failure. BINS. P(X=k) = \binomnk p^k (1-p)^n-k.
 Objective 6.4 - Geometric Distribution: Trials until first success. BITS. P(X=k) = (1-p)^k-1 p.

nodes.title: CED Objective Encyclopedia (Units 7-9 Deep Analysis)
nodes.I:
Objective 7.1 - Sampling Distributions: The distribution of all possible values of a statistic. If n is large, the distribution of x-bar and p-hat is approximately Normal.
 Objective 7.2 - Unbiased Estimators: A statistic whose mean of its sampling distribution equals the true population parameter. p-hat and x-bar are unbiased.
 Objective 8.1 - Confidence Intervals: A range of plausible values for a parameter. Point Estimate +/- Margin of Error.
 Objective 8.2 - Margin of Error: Critical Value \times Standard Error. MoE gets smaller if n increases or confidence level decreases.
 Objective 9.1 - Significance Tests: Evaluation of evidence against a null hypothesis. We assume H0 is true and calculate the probability of getting our result.
 Objective 9.2 - P-values: If the p-value is small (usually < 0.05), we reject the null and have convincing evidence for the alternative.
 Objective 9.3 - Type I and Type II Errors: Type I is a "false positive" (rejecting a true null). Type II is a "false negative" (failing to reject a false null).

nodes.title: The Statistical Tables Archive (Detailed Logic)
nodes.I:
The Z-Table (Standard Normal): Gives the area to the LEFT of a z-score. To find area to the right, do 1 - table value. For negative z-scores, the area is always less than 0.5.
 The T-Table: Used for means when sigma is unknown. You MUST use degrees of freedom (n-1). As df increases, the t-distribution approaches the Z-distribution.
 The Chi-Square Table: Always skewed right and always positive. Area is always in the right tail. df = (rows-1)  (cols-1) for two-way tables.
 How to Read Tables on Exams: If your exact df isn't on the table, use the NEXT LOWER df to be conservative (this makes your p-value larger and harder to reject).

nodes.title: Calculator "Black Box" (The Math Behind the Menus)
nodes.I:
LinReg Math: The calculator solves the "Normal Equations" to find the values of a and b that minimize the sum of squared residuals.
 1-PropZTest Math: The calculator computes z = (p-hat - p0) / sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n). It uses p0 (the null proportion) for the standard deviation calculation, not p-hat.
 T-Test Math: The calculator computes t = (x-bar - mu0) / (s/sqrt(n)). It then uses the t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom to find the p-value.
 normalcdf Math: The calculator uses a high-precision numerical integration algorithm to calculate the area under the bell curve between your lower and upper bounds.

nodes.title: TPS 5e Exam Tip & Caution Archive (The Yellow Boxes)
nodes.I:
Exam Tip (Ch 1): When describing a distribution, always mention the context (e.g., "The distribution of SAT scores...") or you will lose credit.
 Caution (Ch 1): Never use "mean" and "average" interchangeably in technical writing; use "mean" for clarity.
 Exam Tip (Ch 2): Always sketch a Normal curve and shade the area you are calculating. This earns you "Partial" credit even if your final answer is wrong.
 Caution (Ch 2): z-scores only work if the distribution is approximately Normal. Check the Normal Probability Plot first!
 Exam Tip (Ch 3): Interpret the slope as "the predicted change" in y. Never say "the actual change."
 Caution (Ch 3): Correlation (r) does NOT imply causation. A strong relationship can be caused by a lurking variable.
 Exam Tip (Ch 4): In experimental design, specify how you will use a random number generator (e.g., "Assign 01-50 to Group A").
 Caution (Ch 4): Confounding and Bias are different. Bias is a flaw in the system; confounding is an outside variable.
 Exam Tip (Ch 5): Use a tree diagram for any problem involving conditional probability and multiple steps.
 Caution (Ch 5): "Independent" and "Mutually Exclusive" are NOT the same. If two events are mutually exclusive, they CANNOT be independent.
 Exam Tip (Ch 6): When combining random variables, always add variances. Never subtract them, even if you are subtracting the means.
 Caution (Ch 6): Check BINS (Binary, Independent, Number, Success) before using binomial formulas.
 Exam Tip (Ch 7): State the 10% condition (n < 0.10N) before using standard deviation formulas for x-bar or p-hat.
 Caution (Ch 7): The CLT is about the SHAPE of the sampling distribution, not the individual data points.
 Exam Tip (Ch 8): Interpret the confidence LEVEL as what happens in "many, many repeated samples."
 Caution (Ch 8): Never say "There is a 95% probability the true mean is in THIS interval." The mean is either in it or it isn't.
 Exam Tip (Ch 9): State the null and alternative hypotheses in symbols AND in words with context.
 Caution (Ch 9): A high P-value means you "fail to reject" the null. It does NOT mean you "accept" the null.
 Exam Tip (Ch 10): For 2-sample t-tests, do not "pool" the variances unless explicitly told to.
 Caution (Ch 10): H0 for 2-sample tests is always that there is "no difference" (e.g., p1 - p2 = 0).
 Exam Tip (Ch 11): Expected counts for Chi-Square must be at least 5. If not, combine categories if possible.
 Caution (Ch 11): Chi-Square tests are always one-tailed (right tail).
 Exam Tip (Ch 12): Check the residual plot for "no pattern." This is the most important condition for linear regression inference.

nodes.title: Master Common Mistakes Archive (Unit-by-Unit)
nodes.I:
Unit 1 Mistake: Failing to compare centers/spreads using comparison words (higher, lower).
 Unit 2 Mistake: Using the 68-95-99.7 rule for non-Normal data.
 Unit 3 Mistake: Confusing r (correlation) with r^2 (coefficient of determination).
 Unit 4 Mistake: Saying "Random Sampling" when you mean "Random Assignment."
 Unit 5 Mistake: Adding probabilities of events that are not mutually exclusive without subtracting the intersection.
 Unit 6 Mistake: Forgetting to square the standard deviations to get variances before adding them.
 Unit 7 Mistake: Claiming the population is Normal just because n \ge 30.
 Unit 8 Mistake: Including the word "probability" in a confidence interval conclusion.
 Unit 9 Mistake: Reversing the null and alternative hypotheses.
 Unit 10 Mistake: Not checking the "Independent Samples" condition for 2-sample tests.
 Unit 11 Mistake: Using the counts in the table as the expected counts.
 Unit 12 Mistake: Interpreting the y-intercept when x=0 makes no practical sense.

nodes.title: Advanced Statistical Distributions (The Q6 Specialist)
nodes.I:
The Poisson Distribution: Used for counts of events over a period of time or space. Mean = Variance.
 The Exponential Distribution: Models the time between independent events in a Poisson process.
 The F-Distribution: Used in ANOVA to compare three or more means. It is the ratio of two variances.
 The Gamma Distribution: A family of continuous distributions used for waiting times.
 Logistic Regression: Used when the response variable (y) is categorical (e.g. Yes/No).

nodes.title: Exam-Day Panic Checklist (Error Troubleshooting)
nodes.I:
Error: DIM MISMATCH: Occurs when your two lists (L1 and L2) have different numbers of data points. Go to STAT -> Edit and make sure both lists are the same length.
 Error: INVALID DIM: Usually means you are trying to graph a Stat Plot but your lists are empty. Enter data into L1 or turn off Plot1 in the Y= menu.
 Error: STAT PLOT ON: If you try to graph a normal function and see a weird line or box, your Stat Plot is still on. Go to 2nd -> Y= and turn off all plots.
 Error: WINDOW RANGE: Your Xmin is larger than your Xmax. Go to the WINDOW menu and fix the bounds.
 Error: ARGUMENT: You gave a command the wrong number of values (e.g. normalcdf(0, 1) instead of 4 values). Check the help or this manual!
 Empty Residual Plot: If you see no points, you might not have run the LinReg command first. The calculator only updates the RESID list after a regression is calculated.
 Missing r or r-squared: Your Diagnostics are off. Go to the Catalog (2nd -> 0) and run 'DiagnosticOn'.
